solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique, linked answer split by the grid); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Ready for bar, taps unopened winter warmer

parts.note: the two taps on a basin are H and C, hot and cold, joined here by the word 'and'

indicators.note: unopened says the first letter of the warmer is shut away, leaving the rest

parts.note: a muff is a fur tube to keep the hands warm in winter

explanation.surface: A pub-goer, keen for the bar, turns on the taps and pulls off a scarf after the cold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taps' gives H AND C, hot and cold taps, read as letters with the 'and' kept. 'unopened' removes the M from MUFF to leave UFF.
explanation.definitionFit: Putting restraints on a suspect's wrists readies them to stand at the bar of the court, so the verb fits.

clue.text: See 16
Peaches belong to BBC (note flies)

parts.note: to belong to something is to be in it, so belong can give the verb be

indicators.note: flies means the note departs, leaving the rest of the word behind

parts.note: the BBC is nicknamed Auntie, here in the plural with the following 'to' absorbed
N is a note, short for natural in music

explanation.surface: A boast that some celebrity's daughters are owned by the broadcaster, with a musical aside.
explanation.walkthrough: The BBC's British nickname is 'Auntie' (Auntie Beeb); 'note flies' takes N out of AUNTIES to give AUTIES.
explanation.definitionFit: A peach is old slang for a lovely person or thing, so peaches are attractive people or things.

clue.text: Try giving potty up

indicators.note: in a down clue, up says the word for crazy is read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: potty and bats are both informal words meaning crazy

explanation.surface: A parent coaxing a toddler to have a go on the potty.
explanation.definitionFit: To have a stab at something is to attempt it, so a stab is an attempt.

clue.text: See red or, unfortunately, getting ASBO?

parts.note: to see someone is to date them, as is to court them

indicators.note: unfortunately suggests the letters of red or have gone wrong and been rearranged

explanation.surface: A youth who loses their temper ends up with an antisocial behaviour order.
explanation.walkthrough: An ASBO was a British antisocial behaviour order, imposed by a court; the question mark shows it is an example.
explanation.definitionFit: An antisocial behaviour order was one kind of ruling issued by magistrates, hence an example of the category.

clue.text: Snack offered by second actor who's terminated

parts.note: Arnold Schwarzenegger, Arnie, played the Terminator

explanation.surface: A sandwich handed over by an understudy who has just been fired.
explanation.walkthrough: A SARNIE is British slang for a sandwich. 'who's terminated' misleads as sacked: it points to the Terminator films.
explanation.definitionFit: A sandwich is a light meal eaten between main meals, a typical example of a bite to eat.

clue.text: Ding-dong point of view?

parts.note: a ding-dong is a sound of bells, and a bell's sound is a ring; also slang for a fight
a side is one position or opinion in an argument

explanation.surface: Asking where the best view of a fight, a ding-dong, is to be had.
explanation.walkthrough: A ding-dong is British slang for a heated fight, and seats beside a boxing ring give the closest view.
explanation.definitionFit: Seats right beside a boxing arena's ropes give spectators the closest vantage on any bout.

clue.text: I say heading north and not inside is neglect

indicators.note: inside says the word for 'and not' goes within the turned abbreviation
in a down clue, heading north means the abbreviation for 'say' is read upwards

parts.note: eg, for example, is what 'say' means in 'a fruit, say'
nor means and not

explanation.surface: Someone claiming that going north and staying outdoors amounts to neglect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heading north' reverses the abbreviation for 'say' to GE, and 'inside' signals the container.
explanation.definitionFit: To neglect something is to pay it no attention, to overlook or disregard it.

clue.text: Left by half-time — isn't describing complaint

indicators.note: describing is used in the sense of drawing round, so the colloquial word encloses the other pieces

parts.note: ain't is a colloquial form of isn't

indicators.note: half takes the second half of the word time

explanation.surface: A footballer quits the pitch at the interval, though the complaint is that it isn't injury.
explanation.walkthrough: 'describing' is used in its geometric sense of drawing a line round something, so it signals a container; 'half' takes the second half of 'time'.
explanation.definitionFit: A complaint in the medical sense is an illness or disorder, usually a minor one.

clue.text: Very poor rep giving address

parts.note: O is zero, the worst possible score
rep, short for reputation, is one's standing or rating

explanation.surface: A sales rep with a terrible performance score, delivering a speech.
explanation.walkthrough: A zero rating is a very poor reputation; the parse is loose, and the blogger also found it hard.
explanation.definitionFit: Delivering a formal speech is making an oration, so the participle fits giving address.

clue.text: Stuff to go shortly

indicators.note: shortly means the phrase is cut short, losing its final letter

parts.note: to go to the toilet, especially to urinate, is to do a number one

explanation.surface: Packing up items so they can be taken away soon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stuff' misleads as a noun; it is the verb, informal for defeat or cheat.
explanation.definitionFit: To stuff someone, informally, is to trick or beat them thoroughly, which the phrase also means.

clue.text: Turn over, providing sticky stuff

parts.note: a go is a turn in a game
O is the cricket abbreviation for an over

explanation.surface: An instruction to flip something, given in return for some glue.
explanation.walkthrough: An over is a set of six balls in cricket, written O in scorebooks.
explanation.definitionFit: This informal word names any thick sticky substance, a gloopy mess.

clue.text: Where we developed computerised harbours

indicators.note: harbours means the word computerised shelters the letters inside it

explanation.surface: A remark on where computers grew up, in docks run by software.
explanation.definitionFit: Each of us grew as a foetus inside a womb, the plural of which is the Latin form here.

clue.text: Is loner — he's done laps here?

indicators.note: done in the sense of cooked or worked over, so the letters are reworked

parts.note: he, with the 's standing for 'has' and giving no letters

explanation.surface: A lone swimmer has finished their laps and the clue asks where.
explanation.walkthrough: 'laps' is not swimming lengths: water laps the edge of the land.
explanation.definitionFit: Waves lap against the coast, so the boundary between sea and land is where the water laps.

clue.text: Fluid levels see soldier initially revealing guns?

indicators.note: fluid suggests the letters of levels see flow into a new order
initially takes just the opening letter of soldier

explanation.surface: Fluid levels being checked by a soldier, apparently about to show off weapons.
explanation.walkthrough: 'guns' is slang for big arm muscles, not firearms.
explanation.definitionFit: A top with no arms leaves the biceps on display, so it shows off one's muscles.

clue.text: Polish provided German city with rejected bits

indicators.note: rejected bits says each piece is thrown back, so both are read backwards

parts.note: Essen is a city in the Ruhr
if means provided, as in 'provided that'

explanation.surface: Polish is supplied for a German city whose rubbish has been sent back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rejected bits' turns each piece separately: IF becomes FI and ESSEN becomes NESSE.
explanation.definitionFit: Finesse is refinement or elegance of manner, the same as polish in the sense of sophistication.

clue.text: 5 u-turning, eunuch's plea

definitions.meaning: an order from the umpire on a tennis court, referring to the answer at 5
a castrated man wanting his decision reversed would ask for replacement testicles

explanation.surface: A castrated man reverses his court order and makes a plea.
explanation.walkthrough: The umpire calls for fresh tennis balls during a match; the setter said 'u-turning' is the eunuch reversing his decision.
explanation.definitionFit: Both readings rely on the umpire's call for fresh tennis balls, heard literally as a request for new testicles.

clue.text: Loses light vessel — send out for cover

indicators.note: for cover says the rearranged word wraps round the vessel
out means the letters of send are put out of order

parts.note: an ark is a vessel, like Noah's

explanation.surface: A lightship goes dark, and someone is sent out to cover the post.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges the four letters of 'send' into DENS, which 'for cover' then wraps round the vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: When something grows dim or black it loses its brightness.

clue.text: Mounted safer horse, so I heard (drunk, too!), in old country

indicators.note: so I heard says the words are judged by how they sound when spoken

parts.note: someone who mounted a safer horse rode easier

explanation.surface: A boozy tale of riding a gentler horse in a former colony.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drunk, too!' asks for slurred speech, which runs 'rode easier' together. 'so I heard' is also an anagram of the answer, 'drunk' its signal.
explanation.definitionFit: This former British colony in southern Africa is now Zimbabwe, and so a country of the past.

clue.text: Constable's superior genes — art's extraordinary

indicators.note: extraordinary says the letters are taken out of their ordinary order

parts.note: art, with the 's standing for 'is' and giving no letters

explanation.surface: John Constable's painting is better because his genes made his art special.
explanation.walkthrough: Constable looks like the painter; it is the police officer.
explanation.definitionFit: In police ranks this officer sits directly above a constable.

clue.text: From spring, private club for swingers closes

indicators.note: closes in the sense of encloses, so the golf club wraps round the word for private

parts.note: a driver is a golf club, swung by golfers
own means private, as in one's own room

explanation.surface: A private swingers' club shuts up shop when spring comes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'swingers' misleads; they are golfers.
explanation.definitionFit: A river flows away from its spring, so a point lower down the stream lies away from that source.

clue.text: Slack taken up by poor Donk to some degree

indicators.note: in a down clue, taken up means the run is read upwards
to some degree says only part of the words is used, the letters sitting inside them

explanation.surface: The setter, Donk, admits some slackness has been taken up by him.
explanation.walkthrough: Donk is the setter of this puzzle. The letters YPOORD sit in 'by poor Donk' and 'taken up' turns them round.
explanation.definitionFit: Something sagging or hanging loosely has gone slack.

clue.text: Constantly opens up about respect

indicators.note: opens up says the word for about is split apart to take the other piece

parts.note: re means about, concerning
ever means always, constantly

explanation.surface: Someone who keeps talking about respect.
explanation.definitionFit: To revere is to hold in deep respect or esteem, a verb for honouring.

clue.text: Animal spells user's start of password out

indicators.note: out means that letter leaves the wizard's name

parts.note: Harry Potter is a wizard who uses spells

indicators.note: start of takes the first letter of password

explanation.surface: A security warning that an animal is reading out the start of a user's password.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spells' looks like a verb about letters; here it is magic, and the user is Harry Potter.
explanation.definitionFit: This furry river mammal is one kind of creature.

clue.text: What's ending with exhibitionist who's pickled?

definitions.text: What's ending with exhibitionist who's pickled?

indicators.note: ending takes the last letter of What, before the 's

parts.note: Damien Hirst is an artist who exhibits animals preserved in formaldehyde

explanation.surface: Asking what comes to an end when a show-off gets drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: Damien Hirst's best-known works are animals in tanks of preservative; and when a drinker is pickled, the craving for drink has ended.
explanation.definitionFit: Getting drunk ends the craving for drink, so the dryness is what has ended.

clue.text: Eggs on various athletes, only those coming first

indicators.note: only those coming first takes just the leading letter of each word

explanation.surface: Eggs fed to athletes, but only the winners get them.
explanation.definitionFit: This Latin plural names female reproductive cells, as in biology.

clue.text: Give likable rogue local tart

indicators.note: rogue as an adjective means out of control, so the letters run wild

explanation.surface: Advice to tip a lovable rascal at the local bakery.
explanation.walkthrough: This British slang phrase is a crude term for a woman in a small community said to sleep around.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is vulgar slang for a promiscuous woman known to everyone in a small place.

clue.text: Indian city Upper Sixth vacates

indicators.note: vacates means the six leaves the drug's name

parts.note: Viagra is a drug, and an upper is a stimulant
VI is six in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A sixth-form class leaves an Indian city on a school trip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upper Sixth' looks like the final year of an English school; it splits into two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: This city in Uttar Pradesh is home to the Taj Mahal.

clue.text: Pointer, originally — sailor's at sea?

indicators.note: originally takes the first letter of Pointer
at sea means confused, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: sailor, with the 's standing for 'is' and giving no letters

explanation.surface: A sailor lost at sea asks what first pointed the way.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's of sailor's stands for 'is', giving no letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The Pole Star marks north and has long guided sailors navigating by night.

clue.text: Checks instructions for putting siren together

parts.note: split into three short words, the entry is a recipe: the two-letter word for about goes inside a word for wrongdoing, and that builds siren

explanation.surface: A manual tells you how to assemble a siren.
explanation.walkthrough: Split RE IN SIN, the entry is an instruction: put RE (about) in SIN, and SIREN results.
explanation.definitionFit: To curb or restrain something is to check it, a verb pulled from riding.
